Swarm Density Study

Visibility study · ten-drone swarm against one drone

Swarm Density Study

Which cities make the swarm better, or worse, than a single drone at spotting one person in a hat among sixty-four walkers? The study generated cities with controlled clutter and goal layouts, predicted what each interface sees with four tiers of model, and picked three trial levels with a rule fixed in advance. These are the three it picked.

What the codes mean

Every city the study generated is one clutter level joined to one goal geometry, written C·-G·. Three of those combinations became the trial levels L1, L2 and L3.

All 24 levels the simulation tried

Each cell is one clutter level (row) with one goal geometry (column). Its colour is the swarm's advantage at a goal in Tier B: the share of walker-time a pilot can see on the swarm's head-visible feeds, minus the single drone's best realistic policy, in percentage points. Blue: the swarm is ahead. Orange: the single drone is ahead. Click a cell for everything known about it.

The clutter levels: how built-up the city is

Blocks are irregular, generated around random seed points, with streets between them. The buildings are one design from the ScaledCity pack at twice its size, 50 m tall. The maps show seed 0 of each level with today's goal geometry.

The goal geometries: what stands at each goal

Every city has three goals. At each one a central building, the occluder, is ringed by patrolled buildings. Eight walkers circle each patrolled building, and one of all the walkers wears the hat. Drawn to one scale, from real generated goals. The dashed circle is the clearance: how far from the centre the nearest other building stands.

The generated cities

The trial cities for the three picks (seed 101, one of four seeds per level), and one city of every level from the simulation sweep. Drag to pan, Ctrl+scroll or the buttons to zoom, double-click to reset. Hover a goal or a building for its numbers.

Reading the map

North is up. The swarm starts at the triangle, west of the city, and visits the three goals. The small rectangles are buildings and the bands between the blocks are streets. At each goal the largest building in the dashed clearing is the occluder; the ones round it are patrolled by walkers.

At a goal: who sees the walkers

This is Tier B's view of one goal. The swarm arrives from the spawn side and settles round the occluder; the replica of the flight controller decides where each drone ends up. The hull drones' feeds are what the pilot sees on the ring of screens. The single drone flies one of its scripted policies. Walkers circle the patrolled buildings for 60 s. A walker turns the interface's colour while a camera can recognise it: in the field of view, within 40 m, with no building in the way. The ringed walker wears the hat.

Flights in Unity (Tier C)

Recorded flights from the headless Unity bench: the real swarm code, PhysX and the drones' own loss rules, in the trial cities. A scripted pilot flies from the spawn along the streets to each goal in turn, then holds over it for 60 s. One flight also shows the 2-D replica, flown from the same start with the same pilot, so you can see where the two agree and where they part.

Results, tier by tier

Every figure here is drawn from the files the tiers wrote. Hover a mark for its numbers.

G1: the swarm's advantage at a goal, by level (Tier B)

Swarm (best spread, head-visible feeds) minus the single drone (best of its orbits and scan), in percentage points of walker-time. G1 asks for a level at least twice L1's advantage, and one where it vanishes or reverses.

What each interface sees, by goal geometry (Tier B)

The single drone's exposure falls as the occluder grows; the swarm's holds. At the cramped goals (G6, G7) the formation cannot get round the occluder and the single drone does better.

Drones lost per flight in the replica (Tier B')

Spawn to every goal. Losses come at the tight spread, and grow with clutter.

Spacing in transit (Tier B', G2)

Mean distance to the nearest drone. G2 asks for at least 3 m at spread 1.0, the spacing internal_3's collisions came at.

Drones lost per run in Unity (Tier C, G3)

Per run of the trial (spawn, three goals), at the share of tight spread internal_3's pilots flew. Whiskers: the spread over three cities per level. Small marks: the loss per flight at each transit spread on its own.

Where the swarm can surround the occluder (Tier B' envelopment map)

An isolated goal with the formation flown in from 60 m and held over it: the share of settles that envelop, by occluder width and ring radius, at each spread. Empty squares were not built: the ring's buildings cannot keep 5 m from the occluder there.

Free-sight length against coverage (Tier A)

The Boolean model: ℓ, the mean distance a sight line runs before it meets a building, falls as more of the ground is built over. Today's density (C0) is range-limited; the two denser levels are transitional, and the city starts to hide walkers the camera could otherwise recognise. The generated cities use buildings twice today's size throughout; the other two curves show what building size does.

×2, the study's buildings×1, today's buildings×4, not builtC0–C2, measured on the generated citiestoday's two cities (DiamondCityWorld, ScaledCityWorld)

Does the model hold? (Tier A check)

The chance a sight line runs free to 20, 40, 80 or 160 m: the Boolean model (lines) against random scatter cities of the study's buildings (dots). It agrees in open cities and is optimistic in dense ones: buildings that cannot overlap block more sight lines per unit of coverage than the model's, which can.

Everything that ran, and how it was checked

What ran

The replica against Unity

The 2-D replica flew 17 recorded Unity flights per city again, from the same start with the same pilot. It passes when the median track error is within 10% of the path, the spacing within 15%, and the drones lost within 2 per 10 flights of Unity's. How a drone that hits a building is treated decided it.

Watch it happen: the L3 flight at spread 0.4 shows the replica beside Unity.

internal_3: replayed, then predicted

The recorded human runs, scored through the study's camera model, reproduce the analysis to 0.04 s. Predicting them with Tier B's machinery gets the swarm's displayed exposure right and under-predicts the single drone and the head-visible feeds: the pilots did better than the scripted model.

Unit tests

Unity Play-mode check

ProceduralCityWorld played headless on the bench copy, the recorder writing to a scratch folder. All seven passed.

✓Three goals built, with three different hats
✓64 walkers at every goal
✓No walker inside a building after they had walked
✓A swarm reset to 70 m held at 51.3 m, under the 50 m ceiling as flown
✓The session record names the layout, the goal seed and each goal's geometry
✓The new hull, shown and gaze columns are written
✓An RC press far from every goal scored out of zone; one beside a goal scored with its camera distance and feed

Glossary

Every quantity the study uses, with its units. Distances are metres; the city's buildings are 50 m tall.
